source.title: Deep pNML: Predictive Normalized Maximum Likelihood for Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Koby Bibas; Yaniv Fogel; M. Feder

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains a WideResNet-18 with SGD on CIFAR10 whose training labels are randomized at several rates, including fully random labels, and reports training accuracy and test metrics.
record.gate_note: The study's own random-label experiment in Section 4.3 and Table 2 bears on V1 and V4. It does not test training-time overhead, unstructured inputs, explicit regularization effects, or learning order. The pNML and ERM test metrics are reported separately.
record.test_reason: Section 4.3 independently trains WideResNet-18 with SGD on CIFAR10 across label-randomization probabilities, reports perfect training accuracy, and measures ERM test accuracy. These results directly test V1 and V4 despite the experiment's broader purpose of evaluating pNML.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase accurately summarizes Section 4.3: pNML is more robust than ERM to noisy training labels in log-loss, without a significant accuracy difference, and elevated regret can indicate random training labels.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a WideResNet-18 with SGD on CIFAR10 while varying the probability that training labels are random; it uses 350 initial-training epochs and six fine-tuning epochs. It states that no regularization or data augmentation was used. The random-label procedure follows the cited finding, but it does not report a matched true-label versus random-label training-time comparison or establish that all hyperparameters were unchanged from an original setting.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported test accuracy changes with the probability of random labels in the training set.

fits_no_version.finding: pNML improves noisy-label test log-loss relative to ERM, with no significant accuracy difference; its regret helps identify noisy training sets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-specific pNML prediction improves robustness in log-loss, and pNML regret indicates training-label corruption.

record.problems: One model and one dataset are reported for the random-label experiment. No uncertainty estimates are given. The text asserts training accuracy was 1.0 but does not provide separate training-accuracy values by random-label probability; test error at chance is not stated explicitly.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also reports ERM and PNML test loss and regret by random-label probability in Table 2. Those metrics are not extracted because the claim versions concern fit, test error and accuracy degradation, and the accuracy rows directly capture those outcomes.

untested.parts: Relative time to convergence and slowing with increasing corruption; a common 350-epoch budget does not measure either.
Training-set fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian inputs. Gaussian images here are out-of-distribution test inputs.
The mechanism of separating signal learning from noise memorization is not directly measured; the evidence consists of training fit and test-accuracy degradation.
Effects of adding or removing weight decay, dropout, and augmentation are not compared under matched conditions. Section 4.3 uses none throughout.
Learning order and differences between real-label and noise learning over training.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source. The unchanged protocol across corruption levels is described within Section 4.3; matching the original paper's hyperparameters is unnecessary for that comparison. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports that training accuracy was 1.0 and reports test accuracy for fully random labels. It does not report test error explicitly as chance or establish that architecture and all hyperparameters were unchanged from true-label training.
The paper reports perfect training accuracy and test accuracy across six label-randomization probabilities. It does not measure whether the model captures the remaining signal while memorizing noise.
